title: Traditional Kenyan Irio
author: Mama Wanjiru
techniques: How to Preserve Green Colour When Cooking Vegetables

relatedDish.note: Irio and Mukimo are closely related traditional Kikuyu dishes. While the names are sometimes used interchangeably across Kenya, Irio is traditionally mashed more coarsely — keeping individual peas, maize kernels, and flecks of green clearly visible — while Mukimo tends toward a smoother, more unified mash. Both celebrate the same highland ingredients; the difference is in texture and regional emphasis.

heritage.origin: Central Kenya — Kikuyu community, Kenya's central highlands
heritage.history: Irio has nourished Kikuyu families for generations, rooted in the agricultural rhythms of the central highlands where potatoes, maize, peas, and leafy greens grow side by side. Traditionally prepared during harvest seasons using freshly picked ingredients, it was a dish that celebrated the land's abundance. Cooked in clay pots over wood fires and mashed with a wooden mwiko, irio was central to communal meals, family gatherings, and celebrations tied to the harvest calendar.
heritage.modernEvolution: Modern irio frequently uses spinach in place of pumpkin leaves, frozen peas and corn for convenience, and may include butter or cream for richness. It has spread far beyond the Kikuyu heartland and is now served in restaurants across Kenya, often listed alongside Mukimo as a traditional side dish.

desc: Irio is a traditional Kikuyu dish of coarsely mashed potatoes, sweet maize, green peas, and leafy greens — rustic by design, with each ingredient still visible in the finished dish. Hearty, nourishing, and deeply rooted in the highlands of Central Kenya.
longDesc: Where Mukimo aims for a smoother, more unified mash, Irio celebrates texture — each green pea, each sweet kernel of maize, each fleck of spinach should be visible in the final dish. This is the rustic, honest food of the central highlands, born from harvest abundance and prepared with a light hand. Coarsely mashed and simply seasoned, Irio has fed Kikuyu families for generations and continues to comfort and nourish across all of Kenya today.
ingredients: 2 cups (300g) fresh maize kernels — fresh or frozen
1½ cups (225g) green peas — fresh or frozen

substitutions.alternative: Reserved cooking water or plant-based milk

steps: Peel and wash the potatoes, cutting them into even quarters so they cook at the same rate.
Place the potatoes, maize kernels, and peas into a large pot. Cover with cold water, add 1 tsp of salt, and bring to a boil.
Cook for 25–30 minutes until the potatoes are completely tender when pierced with a knife.
Add the chopped spinach or pumpkin leaves in the final 5 minutes of cooking. Stir through and allow to wilt — do not overcook.
Drain most of the cooking water, reserving a cupful in case it is needed for mashing.
Add the butter and milk if using.
Mash gently with a potato masher — the goal is a coarse, rustic texture. Some whole peas, visible maize kernels, and green flecks should remain. This is what makes irio distinct from a smooth mash.
Taste and season with the remaining salt and black pepper.
Mix gently until evenly combined. Serve hot.
chefTips: Use starchy potatoes — they give a lighter, fluffier result than waxy varieties.
The coarse texture is intentional and traditional — do not over-mash. Visible peas and corn are correct.
Freshly harvested maize gives the best natural sweetness. If using frozen, thaw and drain well first.
Add chopped spring onions after mashing for an extra layer of fresh flavour.
commonMistakes: Mashing until completely smooth — this makes it Mukimo, not Irio. The rustic texture is the point.
Overcooking the greens — they turn dull and lose their nutrients and colour.
Adding too much liquid — makes the irio runny and impossible to serve neatly.
Forgetting to taste and adjust seasoning after mashing — the mixture needs a final salt check.
storage: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Freeze for up to 2 months.
reheating: Reheat gently on the stovetop with a splash of water or milk, stirring occasionally until heated through.
healthBenefits: Rich in dietary fibre (7g per serving) — supports healthy digestion.
Excellent source of vitamins A and C from the leafy greens.
Provides complex carbohydrates for sustained energy.
Contains plant-based protein from peas and maize.
Naturally filling and nutrient-dense — a balanced vegetable and starch combination.
culturalNote: Irio has been prepared for generations in the Kikuyu community and is traditionally associated with harvest seasons, family meals, and celebrations in the central highlands. The dish showcases the region's most important crops — potatoes, maize, legumes, and leafy greens — and reflects the agricultural heritage of Kenya's fertile highlands. Today it is enjoyed across the country and is a staple in many restaurants serving traditional Kenyan cuisine.
regionalVariations: Classic potato irio — the traditional Kikuyu version.
Sweet potato irio — partly replacing regular potatoes for natural sweetness.
Pumpkin irio — cooked pumpkin mashed into the mixture.
Bean irio — borlotti or kidney beans added for extra protein.
Spinach irio — heavy on the greens.
Avocado-topped irio — sliced ripe avocado served on top.
Garlic herb irio — roasted garlic mashed in with fresh herbs.
